content: Your doctor has prescribed antihemophilic factor (human), a medication designed to help your blood clot effectively. This medication will be administered either directly into your vein or through an intravenous (IV) fluid that drips into your vein via a needle or catheter. The infusion typically takes about 5 to 10 minutes. The frequency of administration will depend on your doctor’s assessment of your needs, which may be as often as every other day. Antihemophilic factor (human) is a naturally occurring substance in your body that activates clotting factors in your blood to form clots and reduce bleeding episodes. In some cases, this medication may be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Your healthcare provider (doctor, nurse, or pharmacist) may monitor the effectiveness and potential side effects of your treatment through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your symptoms respond to the medication. Precautions Before Administration: Inform your doctor and pharmacist if you have ever had a reaction to antihemophilic factor or if you are allergic to any medications. Notify your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while taking this medication, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental procedures, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking antihemophilic factor (human) before the procedure. Be aware that antihemophilic factor (human) is derived from human plasma. There is a potential risk that it may contain viruses, such as HIV or those causing hepatitis. Discuss these risks with your doctor. Administering Your Medication: Before using antihemophilic factor (human), inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of any floating particles. Gently squeeze the bag or check the container to ensure there are no leaks. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not stop your therapy or alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you experience a mechanical problem, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, stop the infusion and contact your healthcare provider immediately to resume therapy. Side Effects: Minor Side Effects: Antihemophilic factor (human) may cause minor side effects. Notify your healthcare provider if any of the following symptoms are severe or persistent: Dizziness Headache Sore throat Itching Upset stomach Vomiting Fatigue Severe Side Effects: If you experience any of the following severe symptoms, stop the infusion and contact your healthcare provider immediately: Increased pulse rate Hives Unusual bleeding or bruising Difficulty breathing Chest discomfort or tightness Chills Fever If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Storing Your Medication: Your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days’ worth of antihemophilic factor (human) at a time and provide instructions on how to prepare each dose. Store the medication as directed, ensuring you understand the proper storage requirements. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place when not in use, and ensure all medications and supplies are out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In Case of Emergency or Overdose: If you suspect an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Signs of Infection: If you are receiving antihemophilic factor (human) through a vein or under your skin, it is important to recognize the symptoms of a catheter-related infection (an infection at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin).
